blocks.text: Most of the servers we have looked at so far assumed a small, trusted circle of callers. OAuth becomes essential the moment a remote MCP server needs to serve many different clients, on behalf of many different users, over the open internet.
MCP adopted OAuth 2.1 style flows so a remote server never sees a user's actual password, and so access can be scoped, time limited, and revoked without ever touching the user's underlying account.
This lesson walks through the roles involved, the authorization code flow with PKCE, and exactly how a client attaches its access token to every request it sends to a remote MCP server.
1. Why MCP Needed a Real Authorization Protocol

A remote MCP server is just another web service from the network's point of view, reachable by anyone who knows its address. Once a server can act on a user's behalf against real data, a simple shared secret stops being enough protection.

OAuth solves a specific problem, letting a user grant a client limited access to a resource without ever handing that client their password. MCP leans on exactly this model for any server exposed remotely.

Earlier lessons in this module covered Authentication, Authorization, and API Keys as separate building blocks. OAuth combines pieces of all three into one standard flow that many different clients can implement the same way.
2. The Three Roles in OAuth for MCP

blocks.alt: The client, the authorization server, and the resource server are the three OAuth roles

blocks.text: OAuth defines three separate parties, and mixing them up is the most common source of confusion the first time someone reads the spec.

items: Client, the application that wants to call tools on an MCP server on the user's behalf
Authorization server, the service that authenticates the user and issues tokens
Resource server, the MCP server itself, the thing that actually holds the tools and data being protected

blocks.text: In many MCP deployments the authorization server and the resource server are run by the same company, but OAuth does not require that. MCP is deliberately designed so a server can delegate authorization to a separate, dedicated identity provider.
3. What the Resource Server Actually Checks
When a request arrives at the MCP server, its job under OAuth is narrow, validate the access token attached to that request, not know anything about how the user originally logged in.
That validation confirms the token was signed by a trusted authorization server, has not expired, and carries a scope wide enough for the tool being called.

None of this requires the resource server to store a session or remember anything about the login itself, which is exactly why the same MCP server can sit behind many different authorization servers without changing its own request handling logic.
4. Why OAuth 2.1 and Not Classic OAuth 2.0
MCP specifically references OAuth 2.1 rather than the older 2.0 specification, because 2.1 folds a decade of hard learned security fixes into the standard as mandatory rather than optional.

The two biggest changes are that the old implicit grant, which returned tokens directly in a URL fragment, is dropped entirely, and PKCE, once an optional add on, becomes mandatory for every client type, not only mobile apps.

blocks.title: Why this matters for MCP
blocks.content: MCP clients are often installed locally, a desktop app or a command line tool, which makes them exactly the kind of client the old implicit grant used to put at risk. Requiring PKCE for everyone removes that whole category of weakness by default.

blocks.text: 5. The Authorization Code Flow at a High Level

blocks.alt: A client redirects to an authorization server and comes back with a code

blocks.text: The authorization code flow is the pattern MCP relies on, and at a high level it never lets an access token pass through a browser's address bar.

items: The client sends the user to the authorization server's login page
The user authenticates and approves the client's requested access
The authorization server redirects back to the client with a short lived authorization code
The client exchanges that code, privately, for an access token

blocks.text: That last exchange happens over a direct, server style call, never visible in a browser history or a redirect URL, which is what keeps the actual token out of reach of anything watching the browser.
6. Why PKCE Matters for MCP Clients

blocks.alt: A code verifier and code challenge protect the flow with PKCE

blocks.text: PKCE stands for Proof Key for Code Exchange, and it exists to stop a stolen authorization code from being useful to anyone except the client that originally requested it.

Many MCP clients are native applications, a desktop assistant or an editor plugin, and native apps cannot keep a traditional client secret truly secret since anyone can inspect the installed binary. PKCE gives these public clients a safe way to prove their identity without needing a secret at all.
7. How the Code Verifier and Code Challenge Work

Before starting the flow, the client generates a random string called the code verifier and keeps it private. It then derives a code challenge from that verifier using a one way hash, and sends only the challenge in the initial authorize request.

code.content:
import secrets, hashlib, base64

def base64url(data: bytes) -> str:
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).rstrip(b"=").decode()

code_verifier = base64url(secrets.token_bytes(32))
challenge_bytes = hashlib.sha256(code_verifier.encode()).digest()
code_challenge = base64url(challenge_bytes)

# code_verifier stays on the client, never sent until the token exchange
# code_challenge is the only one sent in the initial authorize request

blocks.text: When the client later exchanges its authorization code for a token, it sends the original code verifier along with it. The authorization server hashes that verifier itself and checks the result matches the challenge it was given earlier.
8. Walking Through the Full Flow With PKCE
Put together, the full flow looks the same every time, regardless of which MCP client or which authorization server is involved.

items: Client generates a code verifier and derives a code challenge from it
Client opens the authorization server's login page, sending the code challenge along
User logs in and approves the requested scopes
Authorization server redirects back to the client with a short lived authorization code
Client sends the authorization code plus the original code verifier to the token endpoint
Authorization server checks the verifier against the challenge, then issues an access token and a refresh token

blocks.text: Only after that last step does the client actually have something it can attach to a request against the MCP server.
9. Access Tokens, What They Are and How Long They Last

blocks.alt: An access token is short lived compared to a refresh token

blocks.text: An access token is a short lived credential, often good for anywhere from a few minutes to about an hour, that proves the client has been granted a specific, limited set of permissions.
Because it expires quickly on its own, a leaked access token is a much smaller problem than a leaked long lived API key. The damage window is naturally bounded by the token's own expiry.
Many access tokens are structured as signed JWTs, which lets a resource server verify them on its own without a network call back to the authorization server for every single request.
10. Attaching an Access Token to a Request
Once a client holds a valid access token, using it is simple, it goes in the Authorization header of every request sent to the MCP server, prefixed with the word Bearer.
The resource server reads that header, validates the token, and only then proceeds to handle whatever tool call or resource read the request is asking for.
11. Refresh Tokens and Why They Exist

blocks.alt: A refresh token is exchanged for a new access token without a full re-login

blocks.text: A refresh token is a longer lived credential issued alongside the access token, whose only job is to get a new access token once the current one expires, without forcing the user to log in again.
This is what lets an MCP client stay connected for hours or days at a time while still only ever holding a short lived access token in active use.

blocks.text: 12. Using a Refresh Token to Get a New Access Token
When an access token expires, the client sends its refresh token to the authorization server's token endpoint and receives a new access token back, usually along with a new refresh token as well.

code.content:
POST /oauth/token HTTP/1.1
Host: auth.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=rt_9f8a7b6c&client_id=mcp-desktop-client

blocks.text: This exchange happens silently in the background. From the user's point of view the MCP client just keeps working without ever asking them to log in again.
13. Scopes, Limiting What a Token Can Do

blocks.alt: A scope limits exactly what a token is allowed to do

blocks.text: A scope is a label attached to a token that describes exactly what it is allowed to do, read only access to one tool, write access to another, and nothing beyond that.
A well designed MCP client requests the narrowest scope it can get away with for the task at hand, rather than asking for broad access just in case it turns out to be useful later.

blocks.title: Least privilege by default
blocks.content: If a tool only ever reads calendar events, its token should carry a read only calendar scope, never a broader one that could also write or delete. A stolen token is only as dangerous as the scope it was issued with.

blocks.text: 14. Dynamic Client Registration for MCP Clients

Because anyone can write an MCP client, OAuth for MCP typically supports dynamic client registration, letting a new client register itself with an authorization server automatically instead of a human manually creating credentials in advance.
This matters a lot for MCP specifically, since the ecosystem expects new clients to appear constantly, and forcing every one through a manual registration step would be a serious barrier to adoption.
15. Where Tokens Should and Should Not Be Stored
An access token and a refresh token are both sensitive, and where a client keeps them matters as much as how it obtained them in the first place.

Refresh tokens in particular deserve the same care as a password, kept in an operating system's secure credential storage where possible, never written to a plain log file or a world readable configuration file.

A browser based client has an added constraint, tokens should never be stored in a place ordinary page scripts can read, since a single scripting flaw would otherwise hand an attacker a working credential.
16. What Happens When a Token Is Rejected

If a resource server rejects an access token, expired, malformed, or simply wrong, the correct response is a clear, generic failure telling the client to get a new one, not a detailed explanation of what exactly was wrong with the old one.
A well built MCP client treats this rejection as a signal to attempt a silent refresh first, and only falls back to asking the user to log in again if the refresh itself also fails.
17. How OAuth Differs From a Plain API Key

blocks.alt: OAuth is compared against a plain API key

blocks.text: An API key, covered in the earlier lesson of this module, is usually one long lived secret string that a server compares against a stored value. OAuth instead issues short lived, scoped tokens through a defined flow, and never asks the client to hold a long lived secret at all.

The tradeoff is complexity, OAuth needs an authorization server and a defined flow, while an API key needs almost nothing to get started. MCP tends to reach for OAuth specifically when a server is acting on behalf of many real end users rather than a single trusted operator.

Some deployments end up using both, an API key for trusted server to server automation and OAuth for anything acting on an individual user's behalf, and that combination is a perfectly reasonable design rather than a compromise.
Worked Example

Imagine a remote MCP server that lets a client read a user's calendar. The client first generates a code verifier and challenge, then sends the user to the authorization server with that challenge attached.

The user logs into their calendar provider and approves read only access. The authorization server redirects back with a short lived code, which the client immediately exchanges, along with its original code verifier, for an access token and a refresh token.

From that point on, every call the client makes to list events carries the access token in its Authorization header, and when that token eventually expires, the client quietly uses its refresh token to get a new one without ever interrupting the user.
Common Mistakes

items: Storing a refresh token in plain text next to application logs
Skipping PKCE just because a client happens to have a client secret
Treating a token rejection as fatal instead of first attempting a silent refresh
Requesting a broader scope than the tool actually needs, just in case it helps later
Reusing the same access token indefinitely instead of respecting its stated expiry
Putting an access token in a URL query string instead of the Authorization header

blocks.text: Practice

Pick a small MCP client you control, or build a minimal one, and wire it up to a test authorization server using the authorization code flow with PKCE. Generate a code verifier and challenge yourself, walk through the login and redirect, and confirm the token exchange fails if you send the wrong verifier.

Once you have a working access token, attach it to a request against your MCP server using the Authorization header, then let it expire on purpose and confirm your client correctly uses its refresh token to recover without asking the user to log in again.
Key Takeaway

OAuth gives MCP a standard way to let a client act on a user's behalf against a remote server, without the client ever seeing the user's password and without the server ever trusting one shared long lived secret.

The authorization code flow with PKCE, short lived access tokens, and longer lived refresh tokens work together so a client can stay usefully connected for a long time while keeping the actual window of risk very small.
